---
title: "Planning as a Control Layer"
unit_id: "unit-12"

## A Plan That Survives Contact

The failed gantry trial has produced three obligations. Regenerate the stale
configuration. Diagnose the oscillation. Retest the controller before any
full-speed motion. The desired outcome is clear enough: a controller candidate
whose repository state, simulated behavior, and bounded physical behavior have
all been checked under the current contract.

The first plan is simple. Edit the generator input, rebuild, rerun the
integration test, update the simulator, run another low-energy trial, and then
deploy. Written as a list, it looks complete. It is not.

The generator edit and simulator update can happen in parallel, but both depend
on the same controller contract. The integration test depends on a cold build,
not merely on the source edit. The next physical trial depends on current
sensor calibration, an approved payload, a reachable stop route, and a
controller artifact whose identity matches the build receipt. Deployment
depends on the trial outcome and on authority that no plan can grant itself.
The oscillation diagnosis may change the controller, invalidating work already
done on the generator branch.

A useful plan must represent these facts before execution turns them into
expensive surprises. It needs goals and non-goals, candidate decompositions,
typed dependencies, assumptions, observations, context requests, capability
requirements, resource limits, verification points, stop conditions,
alternatives, and residual owners. It needs to say what can run now, what is
blocked, what may happen in parallel, and what change would invalidate each
decision.

That is planning as a control layer. The plan is not a prediction, a queue, a
worker assignment, or permission to act. It is a versioned policy for ordering
and revising obligations under uncertainty. Its value lies less in describing
one ideal future than in preserving enough structure to change course without
losing the mandate.

## Six Objects That Should Not Collapse

Planning systems often use one word for several distinct objects. Keeping them
separate prevents a graph from inheriting powers it should not have.

A **goal contract** says what outcome is sought, what must not happen, which
parties and rights matter, what authority and resources are available, and
when the mandate expires or requires clarification. Unit 6 established why
this contract is an interpretation under uncertainty rather than a prompt
string.

A **plan** decomposes that accepted contract into obligations and alternatives.
It identifies dependencies, assumptions, observations, validation points,
failure routes, and completion criteria. It can contain branches that will
never execute.

A **schedule** assigns eligible plan nodes to times and resource windows. It
may optimize a critical path, deadline, cost, or burden, but only relative to
the plan model it receives.

A **route proposal** says which capability, model, tool, person, or service
might perform a node under a declared adequacy predicate. Routing owns
qualification and selection among implementations. The planner states what is
needed; it does not certify that a cheap worker is competent.

A **job** is an admitted unit of work handed to an execution system. It binds
specific inputs, outputs, worker state, retry rules, and closure behavior. A
plan node can exist without becoming a job.

An **authority grant** permits a specified actor to attempt a specified effect
inside a bounded envelope. A valid plan and a ready job can still lack that
grant. Reachability is not permission.

For the gantry patch, “run the next physical trial” begins as a plan node. It
becomes schedulable only when the build, simulator, calibration, payload, and
review dependencies are current. Routing may propose the lab controller and a
human observer. Labor or runtime infrastructure may create jobs. A separate
authority owner decides whether the motor command may occur. The plan records
all those requirements without impersonating any of their owners.

## The Plan Begins With a Frozen Contract

A planner should not optimize before it knows which problem it is allowed to
solve. The planning epoch begins by freezing the accepted command version,
consumer, purpose, success obligations, non-goals, authority and rights
ceilings, affected parties, environment, outcome horizon, resource accounts,
support ceiling, and material-change triggers.

The gantry contract requires a verified controller candidate and forbids
full-speed movement before a bounded trial. It preserves the physical stop
route, prohibits using unreviewed generated configuration, limits the available
lab window, and requires that failed predictions and trials remain in the
record. A plan that reaches deployment by dropping the bounded trial is not a
more efficient plan. It solves a different problem.

Freezing does not make the contract eternally correct. It establishes which
version the current plan claims to preserve. A new safety requirement, payload,
deadline, user instruction, or affected-party constraint may require
re-contracting. The planner can propose that change and explain its
consequences. It cannot quietly reinterpret the mandate to keep its schedule
green.

The distinction matters because optimization creates pressure to weaken
constraints that block progress. A system may relabel a required verification
as optional, treat a non-goal as a preference, or infer authority from the fact
that a task appears on the critical path. A versioned contract makes those
moves visible as semantic changes rather than scheduling decisions.

The plan also records abstention as a candidate. “No adequate plan,” “request
clarification,” “defer until observation,” and “use a human-authored plan” are
legitimate outputs. Forcing every planning invocation to return an executable
graph converts uncertainty into invented feasibility.

## Obligations, Not To-Do Items

A plan node is stronger than a task label. “Update simulator” says almost
nothing about what must be preserved. The corresponding obligation identifies
the accepted contract and purpose; exact inputs and outputs; preconditions and
postconditions; forbidden means; observation and context requirements;
authority and rights demand; resource envelope; verifier; expected effects;
failure behavior; fallback; and residual owner.

For example, the simulator update node consumes the current controller model,
payload range, observed oscillation trace, and the world-model residual from
Unit 11. It must produce a versioned candidate model and a comparison report.
It may not overwrite the failed pre-trial prediction. Its verifier checks
whether the candidate reproduces the diagnostic trace and preserves previously
accepted behavior. Failure leaves an owned modeling residual rather than an
empty checkbox.

The cold-build node consumes the exact repository revision and generator
inputs. It produces a content-addressed artifact and dependency receipt. Its
postcondition is not “build command returned zero.” It includes the artifact
identity required by the integration test and physical trial. The node cannot
declare that identity by copying the predicted digest from the plan.

This structure makes partial progress meaningful. The generator fix can be
complete while the controller remains blocked. The simulator can improve while
the physical route remains unauthorized. A failed diagnostic can narrow the
next experiment without satisfying the parent obligation.

It also creates stable repair surfaces. If the payload changes, the plan can
invalidate nodes whose preconditions mention payload while preserving a source
inspection that did not depend on it. Without addressable obligations, systems
often regenerate the whole plan or, worse, preserve every completed step even
when its premises have expired.

## Dependencies Have Types

An arrow in a graph can mean many things. Treating every edge as “must happen
before” hides why the order exists and what a change should invalidate.

A **data dependency** says one node consumes another's output. A **control
dependency** says a decision must occur first. A **semantic dependency** says
an obligation relies on an interpretation or contract. A **temporal dependency**
expresses a deadline, freshness window, or duration. **Authority** and
**rights dependencies** require a current grant or permission. An **evidence
dependency** requires a verifier result. A **resource dependency** requires
capacity. A **state dependency** requires a world or repository condition. A
**recovery dependency** requires a reachable fallback before an attempt.

The edge also records how it was established. It may be asserted by a person,
inferred from a build graph, observed in a trace, imported from a tool, or
unknown. Acyclicity says nothing about truth. A graph can be a perfect DAG and
still omit the generator relation that caused the earlier failure.

For the patch, the physical trial has a data dependency on the controller
artifact, an evidence dependency on integration-test acceptance, a state
dependency on current calibration and payload, an authority dependency on the
lab lease, a temporal dependency on observation freshness, and a recovery
dependency on the stop route. If any one expires, “all predecessors complete”
is not enough.

Typed edges make replanning narrower. A changed deadline may alter scheduling
without invalidating semantic outputs. A changed contract may invalidate nearly
everything. A revoked authority grant blocks dispatch but need not erase a
verified artifact. A failed recovery check can stop the physical branch while
software analysis continues.

Graph form remains useful. A strict topological order over the actual finite
edges excludes cycles in that representation. It can expose parallelism,
critical paths, and blocked dependencies. The discipline is to avoid promoting
that structural fact into completeness, semantic truth, or planning quality.

## Unknown Is a Planning State

Plans fail when missing information is treated as a blank to fill with a
plausible assumption. A governed planner records assumptions, open-world
unknowns, observation provenance, staleness, disagreement, and the consequence
of being wrong.

The gantry plan does not know whether cable flex caused the oscillation. It may
represent several hypotheses and schedule a discriminating low-energy test.
It does not know whether the lab's payload certificate will remain current at
the planned trial time. That becomes a future observation requirement. It may
not know which specialist route can edit the simulator without losing prior
calibration. That becomes a capability request rather than an invented worker.

Missing context can route to retrieval, inspection, sensing, clarification,
human review, deferment, or abstention. Each route has cost and may expose data
or consume authority. Information gathering is itself planned work, not a free
prelude outside the denominator.

This is where Planning consumes Perception and World Models without absorbing
them. Perception supplies bounded observations. World Models supply qualified
branches and residuals. Planning decides which information-gathering or work
obligation follows. It cannot relabel a prediction as an observation or certify
that an observation is true.

Unknown also protects scheduling. A node with an unresolved verifier or route
is not dispatchable merely because idle capacity exists. A scheduler may
reserve a window or rank alternatives, but it cannot turn missing feasibility
into readiness.

## Alternatives Need a Denominator

A planner that reports only its selected graph hides how the decision was made.
Candidate decompositions, rejected branches, retries, timeouts, human edits,
and no-plan options should remain in the denominator.

For the controller patch, one plan repairs the generator first, one diagnoses
the physical model first, one runs both branches in parallel, and one abandons
the controller change in favor of the old qualified version. Another asks a
human engineer to author the diagnostic plan. Each candidate has different
latency, resource, uncertainty, and recovery implications.

Selection records the generator, method, prompt or policy, seed where relevant,
search history, assumptions, expected utility, risk, total cost, and reason for
rejection. This does not make the chosen plan optimal. It prevents the system
from comparing one polished survivor against an invisible set of failures.

Search depth should be consequence- and value-sensitive. A reversible text
edit may justify a direct route. A physical trial with uncertain dynamics may
justify alternatives and explicit contingency branches. More deliberation can
improve a plan, but it also costs time and creates more model-generated
surfaces to verify.

The no-plan baseline is especially important. Sometimes direct reactive
control, a fixed procedure, or an experienced human performs better than a
detailed generated plan. Planning earns activation when its coordination and
anticipation value exceeds its search, verification, delay, and maintenance
cost.

## Reachability Is Not Permission

A planner may prove that a sequence of nodes can reach a target inside its
model. That result says nothing by itself about whether the sequence is
authorized, lawful, acceptable to affected parties, safe, or supported by
current evidence.

Each node therefore carries separate demands for context, capability,
authority, rights, resources, and verification. A node becomes dispatchable
only when its exact dependencies and feasibility predicates are current. Even
then, Planning emits a dispatch request. Runtime and authority owners decide
whether an effect occurs.

This prevents a common escalation path. A planner notices that access to a
restricted environment would shorten the critical path. It inserts an access
node and then treats the graph's dependence on that node as justification for
the permission. The plan has converted convenience into authority.

In the gantry case, the physical trial may be on the only route to empirical
resolution. That fact does not grant a lab lease, authorize movement, or waive
human-presence conditions. If authority is absent, the node remains blocked or
the planner proposes a different route. It may surface the cost of delay; it
may not issue the grant.

The same boundary applies to software tools, personal data, model weights,
publication, spending, and delegation. A plan coordinates obligations under a
ceiling inherited from the contract. It cannot increase that ceiling because
its preferred route requires more power.

## Scheduling the Whole Cost

Once nodes are eligible, scheduling decides when and with which scarce
resources they should run. The familiar objective is critical-path reduction:
shorten the longest dependency chain and total completion time may fall. That
logic is useful, but only relative to the graph and costs the planner has
represented.

The gantry branches compete for more than compute. The simulator update needs a
specialist and a calibrated trace. The cold build needs storage and an isolated
worker. Integration testing needs the lab software environment. The physical
trial needs the gantry, an observer, an authority window, current sensors, and
recovery capacity. Running both branches in parallel may shorten elapsed time
while increasing review collisions or making the shared controller contract
change underneath one branch.

A schedule therefore carries a vector of resources and burdens: compute,
memory, network, tools, credentials, evaluator capacity, human attention,
privacy exposure, rights constraints, energy, physical equipment, recovery
reserve, and opportunity cost. It records slack and deadlines, but it does not
compress unlike resources into one price unless a declared policy justifies
the conversion.

Verification belongs on the critical path when an artifact cannot be consumed
without it. Human review is not free because it occurs outside machine time.
Fallback capacity cannot be sold twice, once as productive capacity and again
as emergency reserve. Retries, coordination, merge repair, and cleanup remain
part of the schedule's observed cost even when the successful trace does not
show them.

The scheduler can propose an optimization: run the cold build while the
specialist examines the oscillation, then join only after both branches bind
the same controller version. It cannot prove that the dependency model is
complete or that the parallel route is worthwhile. Observed completion,
conflict, review burden, and recovery cost must answer those questions later.

## Replanning Is a New Version

When feedback arrives, the planner should not mutate the active graph in place.
It compares the observation with prospective triggers and emits a scoped
replan proposal.

Suppose the cold build reveals that the generator fix changes two additional
artifacts. That observation invalidates the integration-test input and any
downstream physical-trial package. It may not invalidate the simulator's
analysis of cable flex. The replanner computes the affected future subgraph
from typed dependencies, marks stale assumptions and artifacts, preserves
unaffected work only when its premises still hold, and records the old and new
graphs.

The delta explains added, removed, split, merged, blocked, and rescheduled
nodes; changed edges and assumptions; invalidated context, routes, authority,
rights, resources, and verifiers; and new residuals. It also states whether the
accepted contract remains unchanged. If the only feasible route violates the
non-goal or authority ceiling, the correct output is re-contract, escalation,
or failure, not a quiet graph rewrite.

Prospective triggers prevent arbitrary churn. Replan when a material
observation contradicts an assumption, a dependency expires, a route fails, a
resource disappears, a verifier rejects, the contract changes, or a stop rule
fires. Do not replan merely because a generator can imagine another graph.

Replanning itself has cost and can create instability. A fast-changing
environment may invalidate plans before they are checked. Hysteresis, minimum
commitment windows, bounded horizons, reactive subcontrollers, and explicit
abandonment can be better than constant global optimization.

## Branch Joins Are Semantic Decisions

Parallel branches do not become compatible merely because they both finish.
At a join, the planner compares source and state versions, semantic assumptions,
authority and rights ceilings, evidence views, quality predicates, side
effects, resource ledgers, and residuals.

The generator branch may build against controller version 7 while the
oscillation branch produces version 8. Both nodes can be locally valid and
globally incompatible. One branch may assume a 20-kilogram payload while the
other calibrates for 15. One may consume an authority grant that expired
during the parallel run.

A merge can accept one branch, rebuild a descendant, retain variants, request
review, or fail. It should not average contradictory assumptions or choose the
newest timestamp by default. The join receipt names what was compared, which
policy decided, what was rejected, and which residuals remain.

This is another reason plans need semantic identities rather than only task
positions. If an obligation moves in the graph, its identity and descendants
should remain traceable. If two nodes appear similar, equivalence requires
consumer-relative validation, not a matching label or embedding.

The next unit develops the representation machinery for that validation.
Planning decides which obligation should be lowered and when. Cognitive
Compilation must preserve what the obligation means while turning it into a
target artifact or executable job.

## Stop, Fallback, and Recovery Are Work

A plan is incomplete if its failure routes are verbs without mechanisms.
“Stop,” “rollback,” “ask a human,” and “use fallback” each need an owner,
preconditions, timing, resources, authority, descendant handling, verification,
and an observed consequence.

For the physical trial, stopping requires a current control channel and enough
physical margin. Rolling back the software does not reverse motion already
performed or measurements already disclosed. Returning to controller version
7 requires that its artifact, configuration, calibration, and authority remain
available. Human escalation requires an identified person with time and enough
context to decide.

The plan includes these obligations before dispatch. A fallback that becomes
available only after failure is not a reachable fallback. A rollback request
that no runtime can execute is documentation. A stop command that misses its
deadline is a failed effect.

Recovery can also change the future graph. If the low-energy trial stops after
oscillation, descendants are invalidated, the physical state is observed, and
the residual routes back to diagnosis. If stopping leaves the gantry in an
unusual position, the next plan begins from that actual state rather than from
the pre-trial branch.

These distinctions keep planning honest about irreversibility. The graph can
restore a software artifact and still leave external effects, opportunity cost,
human burden, or lost time. Recovery closes only the obligations it actually
satisfies.

## Failure Cases

**The tidy wrong DAG.** Every edge is acyclic and every node is typed, but a
real dependency is missing. Structural validity is mistaken for truth.

**Constraint erosion.** A required verification or non-goal disappears because
it blocks the preferred schedule.

**Reachability laundering.** The planner infers permission from the fact that a
restricted action lies on the only path to the target.

**Capability self-certification.** A route is selected because it is cheap or
available without evidence that it can satisfy the node's adequacy predicate.

**Unknown becomes assumed.** Missing context, observation, or causal structure
is filled with a plausible value to keep the graph executable.

**Alternative survivorship.** Only the chosen plan and completed nodes are
counted; failed searches, retries, abandoned branches, and human repairs vanish.

**Stale completion.** A node remains marked complete after its contract,
dependency, context, model, authority, or verifier changes.

**Global replan churn.** Every observation regenerates the whole graph, wasting
work and making commitments impossible.

**Local replan underreach.** A changed assumption has wider descendants than
the declared repair scope, leaving incompatible work active.

**Blind branch merge.** Two successful branches use different state versions,
assumptions, or authority ceilings and are joined by position or timestamp.

**Paper fallback.** Stop, rollback, recovery, or escalation is named but lacks
a reachable mechanism, owner, deadline, or verification.

**Planning tax exceeds value.** Search, records, reviews, and replanning add
latency and burden while a reactive or fixed procedure performs as well.

Each case demands an observable test. A richer schema can reject some malformed
records. Only task outcomes can show whether planning improves coordination,
recovery, and cost.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

Planning should compete against direct execution, reactive control, fixed
procedures, single-pass prompted plans, ordinary workflows, hierarchical or
symbolic planners where appropriate, and competent human plans. All arms need
the same contract, information, tools, authority, resource ceiling, evaluator
access, and outcome horizon.

For the patch, a strong simple route may be: revert to controller version 7,
perform a cold rebuild, run the full fixed test procedure, and ask the engineer
to diagnose the oscillation separately. It sacrifices parallelism and adaptive
search but may be easier to audit and recover.

The comparison measures useful completion, contract preservation, dependency
errors, unsafe or unauthorized requests, missed help, recovery, rework,
latency, compute, human burden, tool use, false blocks, and residuals. A planner
that looks efficient because its failed searches or human repairs are excluded
has not earned the claim.

Dynamic environments provide the hardest test. If plans expire faster than
they can be validated, a reactive controller with bounded deliberation may be
safer and cheaper. Explicit planning should activate where dependencies,
parallelism, delayed effects, alternatives, and recovery justify its cost.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The current repository implements a substantial finite planning contract, but
not a demonstrated planner.

Seven public proof targets are implemented across two Lean modules. The
Planning module contains 53 theorem declarations, and PlanForge contains 18.
The finite models cover admission, dependency order, dispatch requests,
authority ceilings, stops, versioning, lifecycle transitions, replan deltas,
and residual preservation. Strict topological order over every actual finite
edge excludes cycles in the modeled graph.

The scheduler-state probe contains two valid synthetic scheduler traces and
seven expected-invalid controls. Its graph consumer binds one valid and three
rejected PlanForge cases, five reachable dependency pairs, one thin-summary
collision, and twelve complete graph-transport mutation rejections. The
runtime-replan audit contains two valid synthetic traces and nine
expected-invalid controls.

The complete finite lifecycle reaches renewed job lowering after feedback and
replanning while preserving authority, order, version, stop, dispatch, and
residual invariants. Eleven closed controls reject invalid transitions. These
results establish behavior of the authored records and transition systems.

They do not establish decomposition quality, dependency truth or completeness,
context-demand prediction, selected-route adequacy, scheduler optimality,
useful critical-path improvement, deployed runtime behavior, live-feedback
benefit, safety, transfer, or support promotion. The chapter's core remains
`Design rationale` at `argument` support.

## From a Minimum Planner to a Governed Control Service

A minimum implementation can use one bounded repository task. Freeze the
contract, generate at least a direct route and one decomposed alternative,
represent typed obligations and dependencies, require current context and
route receipts, schedule eligible nodes, record every dispatch request, inject
one material feedback event, compute a replan delta, and verify stop and
residual behavior. Compare it with a fixed workflow and direct execution under
matched resources.

The next stage needs natural tasks with hidden dependencies, changing context,
delayed outcomes, parallel branches, route failures, revoked authority,
resource contention, and recoverable and irreversible effects. Gold labels
must distinguish plan-model error, execution error, observation error, and
evaluation error. Every generated plan, node, edge, retry, timeout, replan,
human intervention, cost, and failure stays in the denominator.

The mature service would choose planning depth by consequence and expected
value. It would combine symbolic constraints, learned world models, search,
human proposals, and reactive policies without giving any one representation
automatic priority. Plans would remain live, versioned artifacts whose
assumptions and descendants expire precisely. Schedulers would account for
compute, tools, verification, privacy, rights, recovery, and human attention,
not merely CPU slots.

Branch joins would compare semantics and external effects. Replanning would be
scoped and causally audited. Stop and fallback routes would be tested in the
environment. The system would learn reusable decompositions only through
governed promotion and retain the slower route when compiled plans drift.

Maturity requires prospective natural campaigns against competent simple,
symbolic, model-based, and human baselines; causal ablations; delayed outcome
measurement; independent evaluation and reproduction; and transfer across
models, tasks, environments, and organizations. A finite DAG proof or clean
trace is the starting contract, not the destination.

## The Strongest Objection

Detailed plans can be obsolete before they are checked. In fast, partially
observed environments, a reactive policy may use current state while a planner
reasons over stale assumptions. More graph structure creates more places for
dependency errors, false precision, and administrative latency.

The objection is correct in some regimes. Planning is not an intelligence tax
that every task must pay. Its activation should depend on delayed effects,
coordination needs, branching, irreversibility, consequence, and the expected
value of information. A low-consequence action with immediate feedback may
need only a short policy and stop rule.

Governance can also become theater. Exact records do not improve a bad
decomposition. A complete denominator does not make search useful. A typed
fallback does not make it reachable. The architecture earns its place only
when it improves outcomes, recovery, or accountability after total costs are
counted.

The practical response is a hybrid hierarchy. Reactive controllers handle
fast local dynamics inside bounded envelopes. Short-horizon planners coordinate
near-term dependencies. Deeper planning activates for expensive, delayed,
multi-party, or hard-to-reverse decisions. Feedback can narrow or abandon the
plan without forcing every control loop through global deliberation.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Dynamic-task studies in which direct reactive control is safer, cheaper, and
more recoverable would narrow when explicit planning should activate. If fixed
workflows or competent human plans match adaptive planning on useful outcomes,
contract preservation, rework, and recovery at lower total cost, the generated
planning layer should contract.

Evidence supporting the broader design would require prospective natural tasks
where the governed route improves joint utility, dependency handling,
appropriate parallelism, stop behavior, and recovery without increasing
unauthorized action, unsafe effects, latency, compute, or human burden. The
study would need matched baselines, complete denominators, causal ablations of
typed edges and replan logic, independent outcomes, reproduction, and transfer.

No one favorable benchmark should turn every task into a planning problem.
The conclusion should remain conditional on task regime, consequence, and
planning rent.

## What This Establishes

A plan is a control artifact for preserving obligations through change. It is
not a polished prediction of one future and not permission to make that future
real.

The gantry plan remains useful because its nodes expose exactly why they are
blocked, which assumptions they consume, and what feedback invalidates them.
The generator branch and oscillation branch can proceed independently where
their premises permit. They cannot merge across controller versions by
convenience. The physical trial stays blocked until its evidence, authority,
state, resource, and recovery dependencies are current.

This structure lets a system replan without rewriting its mandate or erasing
failed alternatives. It also reveals when planning is unnecessary or too
expensive. The measure is not whether the graph is elegant. It is whether the
system coordinates useful work and changes course better than simpler routes.

Plans still cannot execute themselves. Each admitted obligation must be
translated into representations that tools, models, verifiers, and people can
share without losing meaning. Unit 13 follows that translation through
semantic intermediate representations, relational structure, search, and
target lowering.
